description: How rising-edge-triggered D-type flip-flops work as data latches and 1-bit and 2-bit binary counters.
content_html:
Storing a Single Bit

Logic gates process information instantly — their output changes as soon as their inputs change. But digital systems also need to store information: a counter must remember its current count between clock pulses, and a memory circuit must hold data after the input is removed. The simplest storage element in digital electronics is the D-type flip-flop.

The D-Type Flip-Flop

A D-type flip-flop has three inputs — D (data), CLK (clock) — and two complementary outputs, Q and \(\overline{Q}\) (Q-bar). The key property is that it is rising-edge triggered: the flip-flop samples the D input only at the instant the clock signal transitions from LOW to HIGH. At all other times, changes on D have no effect.

Key Fact

At every rising clock edge: Q copies the value of D. Between rising edges: Q holds its stored value regardless of what D does. \(\overline{Q}\) is always the logical opposite of Q.

In symbol form, the D-type is drawn as a rectangle with D and CLK on the left, Q on the right, and \(\overline{Q}\) on the right with a small circle (bubble) to indicate inversion. The clock input is marked with a small triangle to indicate edge-triggering.

Timing Diagram for a D-Type Flip-Flop

A timing diagram shows the D, CLK, Q and \(\overline{Q}\) signals plotted against time. Reading one systematically is a core exam skill.

Consider the following sequence (read each rising clock edge left to right):

Rising edgeD at that momentQ after edgeQ-bar after edge
1st110
2nd001
3rd001
4th110

Between any two consecutive rising edges, Q stays constant — even if D changes. This is the “latch” behaviour: the flip-flop has stored the bit from the previous rising edge and holds it until the next one.

The D-Type as a Data Latch

When a D-type flip-flop is used to hold a data bit so it can be read later, it is described as a data latch. The flip-flop “latches on” to the value of D at the rising clock edge and holds it. This is useful when a sensor produces a brief pulse that would otherwise be lost before a processor can act on it.

Binary Counters from D-Type Flip-Flops

If the \(\overline{Q}\) output of a D-type flip-flop is connected back to its own D input, the circuit divides the input clock frequency by 2. Each rising clock edge causes the flip-flop to toggle — the output alternates between 0 and 1 every clock cycle. This is a 1-bit binary up-counter.

Key Fact

To make a 1-bit binary counter: connect \(\overline{Q}\) back to D. Each rising clock edge causes Q to toggle. The output at Q has half the frequency of the clock input.

The 2-Bit Counter

Two D-type flip-flops connected in series form a 2-bit counter. The Q output of the first flip-flop (Q0) clocks the second flip-flop. Both flip-flops have their \(\overline{Q}\) connected back to their own D input.

The result: Q0 toggles on every rising edge of the external clock (CLK). Q1 toggles on every rising edge of Q0. So:

Clock countQ1Q0Binary value
0000
1011
2102
3113
4000 (reset)

The counter cycles through 0, 1, 2, 3, then resets to 0 — a modulo-4 count. This is a 2-bit binary up-counter. Q0 is the least significant bit (LSB); Q1 is the most significant bit (MSB).

A clock with a frequency of 4 Hz feeds a 2-bit counter made from two D-type flip-flops.

First flip-flop (Q0): toggles at every rising clock edge. Frequency of Q0 = \(4 / 2 = 2\) Hz.

Second flip-flop (Q1): toggles at every rising edge of Q0. Frequency of Q1 = \(2 / 2 = 1\) Hz.

The pattern: each stage divides the previous frequency by 2. If Q0 is connected to an LED, that LED flashes at 2 Hz. If Q1 is connected to an LED, it flashes at 1 Hz — half the rate of Q0’s LED. This frequency-halving at each stage is the key fact examiners test.

If the exam asks for the expected frequency of Q0 and Q1 from a 12 Hz clock:
Q0 = 12 / 2 = 6 Hz
Q1 = 6 / 2 = 3 Hz

A 2-bit counter timing diagram shows four waveforms stacked vertically: CLK (external clock), Q0 (fastest, half CLK frequency), Q1 (slowest, half Q0 frequency).

CLK: a square wave toggling continuously. Q0: toggles at each rising edge of CLK — its period is twice that of CLK. Q1: toggles at each rising edge of Q0 — its period is twice that of Q0 (four times CLK).

To check: count CLK pulses between rising edges of Q1. There should be exactly 4 CLK pulses per Q1 cycle. If you see 4, you have drawn the diagram correctly. Common error: drawing Q1 toggling on Q0’s falling edge instead of its rising edge.
exam_tip_html: The 2-bit counter is one of the most poorly answered topics. Drill these two facts: (1) each D-type stage divides the frequency by 2; (2) the second flip-flop clocks from Q0, not from the external clock. In a timing diagram question, check that Q1 toggles only on the rising edges of Q0. If a question asks for the LED flash frequencies, state Q0 = CLK÷2 and Q1 = CLK÷4 clearly before substituting numbers.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A D-type flip-flop copies D to Q only at the rising clock edge; between edges Q holds its stored value. \(\overline{Q}\) is always the opposite of Q.
  • Connecting \(\overline{Q}\) back to D creates a 1-bit binary counter that divides the clock frequency by 2.
  • Two such flip-flops in series form a 2-bit counter: Q0 runs at CLK÷2 and Q1 at CLK÷4; the counter sequences through 0, 1, 2, 3 before repeating.

practice_questions.text:
A D-type flip-flop has D = 1 when the clock rises. What is the state of Q immediately after the rising edge?
A) 0
B) Unchanged
C) 1
D) Depends on Q-bar
State what is meant by saying a D-type flip-flop is 'rising-edge triggered'.
practice_questions.marks: The flip-flop only samples (or responds to) its D input [1] at the instant the clock signal transitions from LOW to HIGH [1].

practice_questions.text: A D-type flip-flop has its Q-bar output connected back to its D input. The external clock runs at 8 Hz. State the frequency of the Q output and the frequency of the Q-bar output.
practice_questions.marks: Q frequency = 8 / 2 = 4 Hz [1]. Q-bar frequency = 4 Hz (Q-bar is the complement of Q and has the same frequency) [1].

practice_questions.text:
A 2-bit binary up-counter is clocked at 20 Hz.
(a) State the frequency of the Q0 output. [1 mark]
(b) State the frequency of the Q1 output. [1 mark]
(c) Complete the count sequence: the counter cycles through states ___, ___, ___, ___ before repeating. [2 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Q0 = 20 / 2 = 10 Hz [1].
(b) Q1 = 10 / 2 = 5 Hz [1].
(c) 0 (Q1=0,Q0=0), 1 (Q1=0,Q0=1), 2 (Q1=1,Q0=0), 3 (Q1=1,Q0=1) [1 mark for first two; 1 mark for last two in correct order].

practice_questions.text: Draw and complete the timing diagram for a 2-bit binary counter with a clock running at 4 Hz for 1 second. Show waveforms for CLK, Q0 and Q1. (Describe the waveform you would draw rather than producing an image.)
practice_questions.marks: CLK: 4 complete cycles in 1 second (period = 0.25 s) [1]. Q0: 2 complete cycles in 1 second (period = 0.5 s), toggling on each rising edge of CLK [1]. Q1: 1 complete cycle in 1 second (period = 1 s), toggling on each rising edge of Q0 [1]. Q1 is HIGH for the second half of the 1-second interval (from the moment Q0 has its second rising edge) [1].

practice_questions.text:
A 2-bit binary counter is built from two D-type flip-flops. Two LEDs are connected, one to Q0 and one to Q1. The clock is provided by a 555 astable at approximately 10 Hz.
(a) Calculate the expected flash rate of the Q0 LED. [1 mark]
(b) Calculate the expected flash rate of the Q1 LED. [1 mark]
(c) A student observes that the Q1 LED flashes at the same rate as the Q0 LED. Suggest a likely wiring fault and explain why it causes this behaviour. [3 marks]
(d) Explain why it is important that the Q-bar output is connected back to the D input in each flip-flop stage, rather than the Q output. [3 marks]
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Circuit Analysis and Evaluation
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: (a) 10/2 = 5 Hz; (b) 10/4 = 2.5 Hz; (c) Q1 LED flashes at the same rate as Q0 suggests the second flip-flop is being clocked directly from the external clock rather than from Q0 — both then divide the main clock by 2 and run at the same rate; (d) connecting Q-bar to D creates a toggle: at each rising edge, D is the opposite of current Q, so Q flips. If Q were connected back to D instead, D would always equal Q at the clock edge, so Q would never change (it would be stuck at its initial state).
Secure: (a), (b) correct; (c) fault identified; (d) Q vs Q-bar logic explained but not fully.
Developing: (a), (b) correct; qualitative parts incomplete.
Emerging: Only (a) and (b) attempted.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a rising-edge-triggered D-type flip-flop do at the rising clock edge?
flashcard_questions.a: It copies the value of D to Q.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Q hold between rising clock edges in a D-type flip-flop?
flashcard_questions.a: Its previously stored value (it latches the last sampled bit).

flashcard_questions.q: What is Q-bar always equal to in a D-type flip-flop?
How do you connect a D-type flip-flop to make a 1-bit binary counter?
flashcard_questions.a: Connect Q-bar back to the D input.

flashcard_questions.q: A 1-bit binary counter is clocked at 10 Hz. What is the frequency of Q?
In a 2-bit binary counter, what clocks the second flip-flop?
flashcard_questions.a: The Q0 output of the first flip-flop.

flashcard_questions.q: A clock runs at 12 Hz. In a 2-bit counter, what frequencies do Q0 and Q1 produce?
A 2-bit binary counter counts through states: 00, 01, 10, 11, then ___.
What is meant by a data latch?
flashcard_questions.a: A D-type flip-flop used to store a bit so it remains available after the input changes.

flashcard_questions.q: Why would connecting Q (not Q-bar) back to D prevent a D-type from toggling?
flashcard_questions.a: D would equal Q at every clock edge, so Q would never change — it gets stuck in its current state.

glossary_terms.definition: A digital circuit that can store one bit of data; its output retains its last state until a clock edge causes it to sample its D input.
A flip-flop that only changes its outputs at the moment a clock signal transitions from LOW to HIGH, ignoring the D input at all other times.
A D-type flip-flop used to store a single bit of data so that it remains available at the output after the input has changed.
A circuit built from flip-flops that counts upward in binary, advancing by one step on each clock pulse.
